> **Key takeaways**
> - Know your cost floor before you look at anyone else's price.
> - Compare what a class includes, not just the number on the page.
> - Pick one simple price structure, then review it after each term.

## Why pricing a kids' class feels hard

Many small studio owners set their first price by looking at the studio down the road and going a little lower. It feels safe, but it skips the two questions that matter most: what does one session cost you to run, and what do families get for their money?

This method takes those questions in order. You need a notepad, your recent bills and an honest hour.

## Step 1: Find your cost floor

Your cost floor is the lowest price at which a session pays for itself. Below it, every class loses money, however full it is.

Work it out for one session of one class, in five buckets:

- **Room or rent.** Rent, utilities and cleaning, shared across the hours you actually teach. If you hire a room by the hour, use that cost plus any paid setup time.
- **Instructor time.** The class itself plus the time around it: setup, greeting families, tidying, notes. If you teach it yourself, still count your time. A price that only works because you work for free is not a real price.
- **Materials.** Anything a child uses up or takes home, plus a little for spares.
- **Insurance.** Your liability policy and any other cover your business carries, shared across the year's sessions.
- **Admin and tools.** Software, card and booking fees, marketing, bookkeeping, and the hours you spend answering parents.

Add the buckets, then divide by the seats you realistically expect to fill, not the seats in the room. A class that only works when every seat is taken is priced too close to the edge.

That result is your floor. Your price sits above it, with room for a margin, slow weeks and the month when something breaks.

## Step 2: Write down what a session includes

Before you compare yourself with anyone, list what a family actually gets:

- **Length,** group size and how many adults are in the room.
- **The instructor's experience** and any specialty, such as toddlers or kids who need extra support.
- **Materials** included, and anything the child takes home.
- **Progress:** a skill plan across the term, a show at the end, or notes to parents after class.
- **The space:** parking, a waiting area, equipment that is hard to find elsewhere.

This list tells you what to compare in Step 3, and it tells parents why your price is what it is. Our guide on [writing a kids' class listing parents actually book](/blog/how-to-write-a-kids-class-listing-parents-book) shows how to put these points into words.

## Step 3: Compare with similar local classes

Now look outward, at real listings rather than guesses.

- **Search like a parent.** Type the activity, an age and your neighborhood into a map search, and note the classes that come up near you.
- **Open their pages.** Studio websites, booking pages, your city's recreation guide and local marketplaces show prices and details.
- **Compare like with like.** A drop-in and a full term are different products, and so are a large group class and a small one. Work out a rough price per hour for each class and line it up against your Step 2 list in a simple table.

You are not hunting for the cheapest class to beat. You are finding where your class honestly sits. Smaller groups, more experience or more included can justify a price above the middle, if you say why. A newer or simpler class can sit nearer the middle, as long as it stays above your floor.

If similar classes charge less than your floor, don't just match them. Look at your costs again (a cheaper room hour, a different time slot, a slightly bigger group if the activity allows) or change what the class includes.

Across Southern California, rent varies a lot between neighborhoods, so compare with classes your families could realistically drive to.

## Step 4: Choose a price structure

Most kids' classes are sold in one of three ways:

- **Per class.** One price for one session. Easy to understand and compare, and good for workshops and families trying something new.
- **By the term.** One price for a set run of weekly sessions. It helps you plan staff and materials and suits classes that build skills week by week. Make the dates and what is included very clear.
- **Drop-in.** A single visit to an ongoing class. If you also sell terms, it is reasonable to price a drop-in above a term's per-session cost, since single visits are harder to plan around.

Keep it simple. One clear structure beats a menu of options parents have to work out at pick-up.

## Step 5: Think through siblings and trials

**Siblings.** A sibling price can make your class the easy choice for a busy family. Check it against your floor first: the second child still takes a seat, uses materials and needs attention. If a sibling price puts that seat below your floor, you lose money every time it is booked.

**Trials.** A first visit can help a nervous child, and a nervous parent, decide. If you offer one, decide in advance what it leads to, such as a term or a regular weekly spot. Price it on purpose rather than giving a seat away by default, and count trial seats honestly when you work out how many paying seats you fill. The same thinking applies to discounts; our post on [filling open spots in a kids' class without discounting](/blog/how-to-fill-open-spots-in-a-kids-class) goes further.

## Step 6: Review the price after each term

At the end of each term, look at four things:

- **What filled and what didn't.** A class with a waiting list may be underpriced, or just need another time slot. Empty seats may point to a reach problem, not a price problem.
- **Your real costs.** Did rent, materials or pay go up? Redo Step 1 with the new figures.
- **What families said.** Did anyone mention the price? Did families come back?
- **What you changed.** Added materials, a helper or a show? Your price can reflect that.

When you change a price, tell current families before the new term opens and explain why. Small, regular steps are easier to accept than a big jump after years of standing still.

## FAQ

### How do I work out what one kids' class costs me to run?

Add room or rent, instructor time including setup, materials, insurance and admin for one session, then divide by the seats you expect to fill. That is your floor; your price sits above it.

### Should I price my class lower than nearby studios?

Not by default. Compare what each class includes and price where yours honestly sits, always above your cost floor.

### Is it better to charge per class or by the term?

Per class is easy to try and compare. A term suits skill-building classes and helps you plan. Choose one clear structure.

### Should I offer a sibling price?

Only if the sibling seat still covers your cost floor. On ORYN Quest, the sibling discount is one ORYN pays for, so it doesn't cut your pay.

### How often should I review my prices?

After each term. Check what filled, your costs and what families said, and announce any change before the new term opens.
